Today is the tenth lecture, where we will explore low-voltage systems. In North America, there is typically no distinction made between low-voltage and high-voltage systems, but large design firms still specialize in low-voltage system design. Many small and medium-sized consulting firms handle both low-voltage and high-voltage projects.

It’s important to note that low-voltage systems generally do not include security alarm systems.

The alarm system belongs to the high-voltage electrical section. This content is divided into two parts: the first part introduces the communication system and other related systems, while the second part will focus on discussing the design of the security system.

The design of communication systems primarily involves telecommunication infrastructure, rather than the software or architectural design within the system. The infrastructure includes the following aspects:

The design of communication systems primarily involves telecommunication infrastructure, rather than the software or architectural design within the system. The infrastructure includes the following aspects:

Power Distribution: How to supply power to the communication system.

Equipment Cabling: Includes the methods for laying power and communication cables, such as pathway planning or rough-in.

Grounding and Bonding: Refers to the grounding system.

Telecommunication Spaces: Such as the size requirements and air conditioning configuration of telecommunication rooms. This typically refers to inter-floor telecommunication spaces, while large Data Centers are more specialized and complex.

Telecommunication Spaces: Such as the size requirements and air conditioning configuration of telecommunication rooms. This typically refers to inter-floor telecommunication spaces, while large Data Centers are more specialized and complex.

The following aspects are generally not within the scope of electrical or low-voltage engineers’ responsibilities:
- Selection or design of telecommunication equipment (e.g., servers, routers, switches).
- Cabling between devices, though relevant standards must be understood. For example, the maximum transmission distance for Ethernet cables (Cat5/Cat6) should not exceed 100 meters, with practical installations often limited to 90 meters.
- Network topology, software configuration, and termination testing, among others.

This division of responsibilities is common in North America, though specific divisions in the IT field may vary.

This division of responsibilities is common in North America, though specific divisions in the IT field may vary.

The relevant norms and standards in the United States are established by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI).

There are two main industry association standards: one is TIA (Telecommunications Industry Association), and the other is EIA (Electronic Industries Alliance). Additionally, there is a global industry association called BICSI (Building Industry Consulting Service International). TIA and EIA standards are primarily applicable within the United States, while other countries like Canada adopt the CSA (Canadian Standards Association) standards. These organizations often reference each other’s standards.

BICSI is an association focused on low-voltage systems and has published numerous design guidelines. It offers a professional certification—RCDD (Registered Communication Distribution Designer)—which is typically required for telecommunications design work. The RCDD certification remains essential for major projects.  

In Canada, the telecommunications field largely follows U.S. standards. BICSI’s influence extends beyond North America, reaching Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Asia. The organization provides extensive design guidelines and standards for data center design. The RCDD exam is quite challenging, taking four to five hours to complete; one exam consists of 280 questions.

The standards most relevant to us pertain to cabling, including cable installation and pathway design, covering conduits and cable trays, among other aspects.

Grounding and bonding are essential concepts in electrical engineering that need to be understood and properly configured. This area has detailed standards, such as administration, among others. Although it may not be directly relevant to us, a general understanding is sufficient.

Relevant standards include those from the Electronic Industries Alliance (EIA) and the Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA), among others.

The first standard pertains to the method of cable installation. The second standard is similar to the first, both covering specific steps of cable laying.

The first standard pertains to the method of cable installation. The second standard is similar to the first, both covering specific steps of cable laying.

The first standard is Generic Telecommunications Cabling for Customer Premises, applicable to customer-owned premises. The second standard is Commercial Building Telecommunications Cabling Standard, specifically targeting cabling systems within commercial buildings. This is similar to the domestic concept of “structured cabling,” which integrates all systems through centralized wiring.

The third standard is Optical Fiber Cabling Components Standard, primarily specifying technical requirements for fiber optic cabling and its components. The fourth standard, Commercial Building Standard for Telecommunications Pathways and Spaces, details installation specifications for facilities such as communication rooms, cable trays, and conduits.

Next, we will introduce the Grounding Standards and the Administration Standard for the Commercial Telecommunications Infrastructure. This standard covers the connection methods for telecommunications equipment such as patch panels, but this part is not highly relevant to us.

The aforementioned standards belong to the TIA Series, and it can be seen that these standards are developed by the TIA and ANSI National Standards Committee. The following similar standards are jointly issued by TIA and EIA, for example:
- The second item, Commercial Building Telecommunications Cabling Standard Part 2: Balanced Twisted-Pair Cabling Components, is the Wiring Standard;
- The third item, Commercial Building Telecommunications Cabling Standard Part 1: General Requirements, is the General Standard for cable installation.

This is the relevant standard for optical fiber cables, including testing standards. Additionally, there are standards regarding the color coding of optical fiber cables.

Canada has some standards, but mainly follows those of the United States. In North America, there are typically so-called service provider standards. For example, Canada has Telus, Shaw, and Rogers, while the U.S. has internet or cable providers like Bell and Verizon, each of which has established certain standards.

When designing, it is necessary to comply with the requirements of the local communication service providers. For instance, when designing in Vancouver, one must adhere to the specific requirements of local service providers for communication equipment, such as the dimensions of communication backplanes.

Additionally, the BICSI Design Guidelines provide detailed design specifications. In another course, I once explained the key reference materials for both North American countries, which included content from the BICSI Design Guidelines, covering telecommunication systems in commercial buildings.

The following is a brief introduction to hardware equipment. Hardware primarily includes servers, routers, switches, hubs, patch panels, as well as software and communication protocols. Additionally, the infrastructure section covers the aforementioned components and extends to lighting systems, fire alarm systems, and access control systems, all of which fall within our design scope.

The main function of the telecommunication system is to provide high-quality transmission of voice, data, and video signals throughout the entire building. Transmission media mainly consist of the following types: cables (including copper twisted pairs such as Ethernet cables), optical fibers (divided into multimode and single-mode), as well as wireless and satellite communication. Strictly speaking, satellite communication differs from wireless communication; here, wireless primarily refers to WiFi, while satellite communication denotes communication between mobile phones and satellites.

Network types include local area networks (LANs), wide area networks (WANs), and the internet, with 5G networks now also in use. System complexity can range from small server rooms to large-scale data centers.

Network types include local area networks (LANs), wide area networks (WANs), and the internet, with 5G networks now also in use. System complexity can range from small server rooms to large-scale data centers.

Next, we will discuss the design of telecommunication systems. For electrical engineers, some aspects of this content may fall outside their professional scope, as it primarily involves the work domain of telecommunication designers.

The design of telecommunication spaces requires coordination with architectural, mechanical, or client teams to determine the location, quantity, and size of these spaces. This includes specific requirements for the building, such as fire protection measures, door and window placement, ceiling height, and layout. The HVAC system must also meet certain criteria, such as maintaining temperatures below 26°C and providing adequate airflow.

In large buildings, telecommunication systems often require backup power, especially in critical areas like design centers, where requirements are more stringent. For power distribution, aside from backup power, systems can be categorized into different tiers based on project importance, complexity, and scale. Tier 4 represents the highest level, featuring fully redundant designs with backups for every component. Cable routing and tray layouts within telecommunication spaces must adhere to specific standards, typically employing PDU power distribution systems and dedicated outlets, with all servers connected to these PDUs.

The lighting system must meet high illumination requirements, including general and emergency lighting. For fire alarm and access control systems, smoke detectors or alarm devices must be installed in telecommunication rooms. In large data centers, due to the high value of server equipment, gas-based fire suppression systems may be used instead of water sprinklers. These systems feature independent fire alarm panels integrated with the building’s fire alarm system while maintaining complete fire detection and suppression capabilities—essentially a unified fire alarm and suppression design.

For security reasons, data centers, telecommunication rooms, and server rooms do not allow unauthorized access, so an access control system is typically required.

Pathway and rough-in involves the installation methods of cable trays or conduits.

For security reasons, data centers, telecommunication rooms, and server rooms do not allow unauthorized access, so an access control system is typically required.

Pathway and rough-in involves the installation methods of cable trays or conduits.

Grounding and bonding are particularly critical in telecommunication systems, where the requirements for equipotential bonding and grounding exceed those of standard buildings, and grounding resistance must meet stricter regulations. Additionally, the design of the grounding system has special requirements, with detailed standards outlined in industry guidelines (e.g., the BICSI Guide).

For large-scale projects, designers are usually required to hold RCDD (Registered Communications Distribution Designer) certification.

Telecommunication spaces include entrance facilities, telecommunication rooms, or telecommunication equipment rooms.

Telecommunication spaces include entrance facilities, telecommunication rooms, or telecommunication equipment rooms.

During the initial design phase, determining equipment locations must be based on building type. Typically, these devices are situated on the first floor or in the basement. Considerations include the number of cabinets and servers, network design, and providing dimensions and category information to the architectural discipline.

In residential projects, dedicated telecom spaces are usually absent, and they are shared with electrical rooms. For large-scale projects, the most coordination is required with the client’s IT department. As end-users, the IT department has a comprehensive understanding and vision of the company’s or system’s IT infrastructure, thus raising numerous critical requirements.

Additionally, coordination with the architectural discipline is necessary. The mechanical discipline must ensure that temperature and humidity within telecom spaces are maintained within specific ranges. For the power supply system, emergency power and UPS units must be provided.

The Backup Time of a UPS refers to the duration it can continue operating after a power outage, which is a crucial criterion when selecting a UPS. The backup time should not be excessively long, as this would require batteries that occupy too much space.

Regarding Redundancy, data centers are classified into four tiers. Another metric for evaluating data centers is Shutdown Time, which refers to the allowable system maintenance time within a year. Different tiers of data centers have varying requirements for this, with higher-tier data centers potentially permitting only a few minutes of maintenance downtime.

The shutdown time discussed refers to the annual unavailability of the infrastructure power supply system, typically requiring an availability rate of 99.99%, meaning only 1-2 hours of downtime per year is allowed. For Tier 4 data centers, their backup systems must ensure extremely short downtime.

In data center design, load calculation differs from that of typical commercial buildings. Due to the high power consumption and heat generation of servers, the power load per square meter can exceed 1000 watts, far surpassing the standard of 100-200 watts per square meter for ordinary buildings. For example, Bitcoin mining equipment is a typical high-density computing device.

Redundancy design and PDU (Power Distribution Unit) have been explained earlier. Additionally, public systems also require Emergency Power. When coordinating with mechanical engineering disciplines, the total heat generation of server rooms or data centers must be calculated based on the number of servers and the heat generation parameters specified in their technical specifications, to facilitate the design of the air conditioning system by the mechanical team.

Regarding lighting design, the primary considerations are the presence of numerous cable trays, air conditioning vents, and various cables in server rooms or communication spaces. Therefore, the installation location of lighting fixtures is crucial to avoid conflicts with other facilities.

Fair Line Assets Control once mentioned Pathway Rough-In, which includes various cabling methods. The most common practice is laying communication cables within cable trays, which is the industry standard.

Fair Line Assets Control once mentioned Pathway Rough-In, which includes various cabling methods. The most common practice is laying communication cables within cable trays, which is the industry standard.

Additionally, wiring within cable trays primarily serves public areas such as corridors. When extending from corridors to individual rooms—especially to each workstation—conduits are typically routed along walls. Another method involves using J-hooks, which allows for free-air cabling.

Above office spaces, there is usually a suspended ceiling, referred to as a T-bar grid, commonly in 2×4 configurations. Between the concrete ceiling and the suspended ceiling, communication cables are often installed. These cables can be directly hung on J-hooks without the need for conduits or cable trays. While this approach is permissible in certain scenarios, it is recommended to prioritize conduits or cable trays to provide mechanical protection.

For in-office cabling, the traditional method employs service poles—square ducts extending from the suspended ceiling to each workstation, containing both power and communication cables, with terminals connected to outlets.

Regarding communication entry lines, due to the high volume of external cables entering the building, coordination with other utilities (e.g., water pipes, gas pipes, or electrical conduits) is essential to avoid crossings and conflicts. Grounding and bonding systems have been previously introduced.

In telecommunications equipment rooms, a grounding bus is typically installed, and its specifications must comply with strict industry standards. Additionally, the cable trays and conduits within the equipment room also require grounding.

In certain cases, an isolated grounding method may be employed, primarily for equipment that could potentially interfere with control systems. However, telecommunications equipment generally does not require isolated grounding.

In certain cases, an isolated grounding method may be employed, primarily for equipment that could potentially interfere with control systems. However, telecommunications equipment generally does not require isolated grounding.

The above covers the key points regarding grounding design in telecommunications systems. Next, we will discuss other aspects related to communication systems.

Among other systems, the Public Addressing System (PAS) is widely used in places such as airports, train stations, and schools. This system is primarily employed for broadcasting announcements or playing background music. Its structure is relatively simple, mainly consisting of components like system diagrams, microphones, amplifiers, players, and recording devices. The system layout design must consider factors such as sound pressure level, coverage area, room partitions, and ceiling height to determine the quantity and placement of speakers.

The system is equipped with a microphone for broadcasting operations and supports selecting different zones for partitioned broadcasting. The amplifier needs to be used in conjunction with mobile audio equipment. There are various types of speakers, including ceiling-mounted speakers and horn column speakers.

Next, the intercom system will be introduced.

This intercom system is primarily used in residential buildings and has been widely adopted in both domestic communities and international markets. Early intercom systems utilized telephone lines to achieve basic voice communication, while modern systems have been upgraded to video intercoms with visual capabilities.

The system mainly consists of the following components: dialing pad, controller, microphone, and display, among others. Its communication typically relies on the building’s telephone system as the transmission medium to enable echo communication.

The system is interconnected with the building access control system and alarm system, requiring integration. Its power and grounding requirements are similar to those of a PA system, but due to its application in residential projects, the technical specifications are relatively more lenient.

The second part of today’s lesson will cover the design of security systems. This section is quite technical. First, I’ll provide an overview of the overall architecture of security systems, followed by an introduction to relevant codes and standard specifications.

In addition, the equipment and components, system design, and testing and debugging of security systems are also crucial aspects. The importance of security systems is self-evident—whether it’s national-level conference centers, capitol buildings, government offices, or private residences, all require appropriate security systems.

Security systems are essential for every building or project, especially for projects like CPD. A security system primarily consists of three components:

First is the Access Control System, followed by the Camera System, also known as CCTV Video Surveillance. The third component is the Intrusion Detection System, or Alarm System, which triggers an alert upon unauthorized entry, notifying security personnel or the police.

Typically, these three components are not standalone. Some projects may only deploy an access control system, while others might install just a camera system or an alarm system. However, in most cases, two or all three systems are integrated. Hence, system integration becomes crucial. Many manufacturers offer combined hardware and software solutions for all three systems, while those specializing in a single system are relatively rare.

Internationally, especially in large-scale projects, security system design is typically divided into two phases:  
1. A security consultant conducts preliminary work, including risk assessment and threat analysis, and develops a security plan based on the project type and the owner’s requirements.  
2. A detailed design engineer is then responsible for specific implementation, determining the installation locations of sensors, cameras, and anti-theft devices, as well as system selection.

Broadly speaking, security systems can be divided into several main components:
- Electronic Security System (ESS)
- Physical protection measures, such as reinforced walls in bank vaults and other physical security facilities
- Security personnel, such as guards stationed within buildings

When planning and designing a security system, different levels of protection must be established based on the project’s importance and unique characteristics. For example:
- Ordinary buildings may only require a single layer of protection
- Campus projects like those in a Central Business District (CBD) may employ a multi-layered protection system:
- The perimeter is equipped with the first line of defense (e.g., security checks at entry points)
- The core areas are then secured with a second layer of protection

Within the core area of the building, there is a security system in place. Whether it’s personnel or equipment, once inside the building, the internal core area requires higher-level security measures. These are all issues that need to be considered during the security system planning phase.

Below I will introduce the common components of an access control system. An access control system typically includes the following components:

Door Contact: A contact sensor installed between the door and the door frame. When the door is closed, the contact remains connected; when the door is opened, the contact disconnects, sending different signals to the control unit to monitor the door’s open/close status.

Card Reader: A device used for swiping cards to gain entry.

Request for Exit: A sensor installed above the door, usually employing a motion sensor or infrared sensor. When someone exits from the inside, the system does not trigger an alarm, distinguishing it from external intrusion scenarios.

Door Closer/Opener: An automatic door-closing device, which may use a spring mechanism or motor drive. Some devices also include an opening function.

Door Closer/Opener: An automatic door-closing device, which may use a spring mechanism or motor drive. Some devices also include an opening function.

Push Button: Primarily designed for disabled individuals, this button opens the door when pressed. The system simultaneously activates the motor and releases the door lock (such as a magnetic lock or electric strike) to ensure smooth door opening. If the lock is not released, motor operation may cause equipment damage.

Panic Bar: An emergency push bar that allows people to open the door from the inside by pushing it in emergency situations.

These components together form a complete access control system, ensuring both security and convenience.
